newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - Home within the range.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - Home within the range.

text.p: Conservative moves should be the rule for the U.S. credit markets on Wednesday, leaving fixed-income instruments to mark a narrow band ahead of September payrolls on Friday, analysts said.

The 1000 EDT/1400 GMT release of construction spending for August may provide fodder for some price fluctuations, however, in light of surprisingly strong August home sales reported on Monday, some said. New home sales rose to an annual rate of 832,000 in August from 795,000 rate in July, the Commerce Department said.
In a Reuters survey, the average forecast of economists expect construction spending rose 0.8 percent in August versus the sharp 1.4 percent decline reported for July.

"There's not much data but construction data could be interesting to see how much the sales results will filter in over the past couple months," said Matthew Alexy, chief market strategist at CS First Boston.

Cary Leahey, senior economist at Lehman Brothers, said construction data will have to post an increase of near 1.0 percent to capture market attention, however, given the data's volatile nature and participants' preoccupation with payrolls.

Away from economic data, Alexy said he expects major price moves will be capped as players stick to conservative bets in front of the traditionally potent jobs data. Range for the December T-bond contract should hold between the mid-109s to 110-10, he said, while the 30-year bond should stick within 6.84 percent and 6.95 percent.
"The market's not going to get too far ahead or too far behind the curve until the employment number," Alexy said, adding that the markets are probably close to the high end of the current range.

Talk of an Australian financial newspaper story which reported that Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan did not see U.S. inflation as a near-term problem may have bolstered market tone, Alexy said, but it was also unlikely to break the psychological hold of employment data.

"The meeting is still so far away and we have one more employment report between the next FOMC meeting and now - this one and in early November - so there's quite a bit of data to be looked at," Alexy said.
Analysts said they expect little, if any, market reaction to the Treasury's ten-year note auction announcement.

With the magnitude of a third quarter rebound in question, Lehman's Leahey said the market will keep a close watch on the rate-sensitive auto sector. The market is expecting a "good" car sales figure of at least 725 million units, he noted.

"Housing and motor vehicle demand remain pretty strong so if you get any surprise (in auto sales) or if the construction data looks strong, it might bother the market a little," Leahey said, adding the market's tenor is good.

Fixed-income markets ratcheted higher on Tuesday after the National Association of Purchasing Managers said its index of manufacturing activity fell to 51.7 in September, below forecasts of 52.5. The index read 52.6 in August.
Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp, said the NAPM set a good tone for the market but that a further surge in Treasury prices is not in the cards.
"The purchasing managers report and the employment report often go in different directions and I would just look for a stable tone until Friday, Johnson noted.
"Friday's report will determine whether we are going to break out of the important range and that is 6.70 percent on the low side, 7.25 percent on the high side," he added.
